meta.name: Witnessed Choking — Cardiac Arrest from Foreign Body Airway Obstruction

patient.name: Gregory Halvorsen
patient.chiefComplaint: Unresponsive, witnessed choking during a meal

history.hpi: Patient was eating a steak dinner with a coworker when he suddenly stood up, grabbed his throat, and could not speak or cough. He collapsed within about a minute. The coworker attempted abdominal thrusts without success before the patient became unresponsive and stopped breathing; 911 was called immediately.
history.lastOralIntake: Currently eating dinner (steak) at time of event
history.events: Witnessed choking on food at a restaurant table, coworker attempted abdominal thrusts, patient became unresponsive and apneic

scene.location: Restaurant dining room, patient supine on the floor beside his table, cleared space around him
scene.safety: No hazards to crew noted; restaurant staff have cleared bystanders and moved furniture
scene.bystanders: Coworker present, witnessed the choking event and attempted abdominal thrusts before EMS arrival; restaurant manager assisting with scene access
visualCues: Patient supine on restaurant floor, unresponsive
No visible chest rise, cyanotic lips
Partially chewed food visible at the mouth
Overturned chair and scattered napkins near the table

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 58-year-old male supine and unresponsive on the restaurant floor following a witnessed choking event. He is apneic with no palpable pulse and visible food debris at the mouth.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Obstructed; food debris visible at the mouth, no air movement felt or heard
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No palpable carotid or radial pulse
otherFindings: Partially chewed food visible in the oropharynx
Coworker reports collapse occurred within the last 1-2 minutes

transitions.condition: Crew immediately begins high-quality chest compressions while a second provider performs direct laryngoscopy to visualize and suction the obstructing food bolus, then achieves effective bag-valve-mask ventilation.
Crew attempts bag-valve-mask ventilation without first visualizing and clearing the obstructing food bolus, resulting in no chest rise and continued hypoxia despite compressions.

phases.name: CPR started, airway obstruction cleared
phases.description: Crew initiates immediate high-quality chest compressions while simultaneously managing the obstructed airway: direct laryngoscopy visualizes the food bolus, which is suctioned/cleared, allowing effective two-person BVM ventilation with continuous waveform capnography in place.
phases.triggerCondition: Given the witnessed choking with subsequent cardiac arrest, the crew recognizes a respiratory etiology and prioritizes early, deliberate airway management alongside compressions rather than deferring airway care as in a typical cardiac-etiology arrest.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Cleared of visible obstruction via direct laryngoscopy and suction
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic, effective BVM ventilation with visible chest rise
otherFindings: Food bolus visualized and cleared from the oropharynx under direct laryngoscopy
Chest rise now visible with each BVM ventilation

expectedActions.shortAction: Begin immediate high-quality chest compressions, minimally interrupted
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Successful resuscitation from cardiac arrest depends primarily on effective, minimally interrupted chest compressions and prompt defibrillation if the patient is in pulseless VT/VF. Arrests of respiratory etiology (including drowning). In addition to the above, consider early management of the patient's airway
expectedActions.rationale: Chest compressions remain the priority even in an arrest of respiratory etiology; airway care is escalated early alongside them rather than delayed.

expectedActions.shortAction: Perform direct laryngoscopy to visualize the oropharynx; suction and clear the obstructing food bolus (SALAD technique)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Airway obstruction with foreign body or swelling (e.g., angioedema, posterior pharyngeal and laryngeal infections). Suction airway: for significantly contaminated airways, consider utilizing a suction assisted laryngeal airway decontamination (SALAD) technique
expectedActions.rationale: Ventilation cannot be effective until the obstructing foreign body is visualized and removed from the airway.

expectedActions.shortAction: Provide two-person, two-thumbs-up BVM ventilation once the airway is cleared, with PEEP
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Use bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation in the setting of respiratory failure or arrest. Two-person, two-thumbs-up BVM ventilation is preferred. PEEP should be used with BVM
expectedActions.rationale: Two-person BVM technique with PEEP maximizes effective ventilation once the airway is patent.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply continuous waveform capnography to monitor CPR quality and detect ROSC
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Is strongly encouraged in patients in cardiac arrest to monitor quality of CPR, as an early indicator of ROSC (rapid increase of 10-15 in EtCO2)
expectedActions.rationale: A rapid rise in EtCO2 is an early, reliable indicator of return of spontaneous circulation.

transitions.condition: With the airway cleared and effective ventilation and compressions ongoing, EtCO2 rises sharply and a palpable pulse returns.

phases.name: ROSC achieved after airway cleared
phases.description: Following successful clearance of the airway obstruction and effective CPR, the patient achieves return of spontaneous circulation. Crew transitions to post-ROSC care, securing the airway, avoiding hyperventilation, and closely monitoring for re-arrest.
phases.triggerCondition: EtCO2 rises sharply and a palpable pulse returns, indicating return of spontaneous circulation after the airway obstruction was cleared.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, secured with supraglottic airway, chest rise present
otherFindings: EtCO2 rose sharply from 14 to 38 mmHg, consistent with ROSC
Continuous cardiac and capnography monitoring maintained

expectedActions.shortAction: Secure the airway and support ventilation, avoiding hyperoxygenation (target SpO2 94-98%)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Secure airway. Administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94-98% saturation. Do not hyperoxygenate
expectedActions.rationale: Post-ROSC hyperoxygenation is associated with worse neurologic outcomes; titrated oxygen is preferred.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

expectedActions.shortAction: Ventilate at 8-10 breaths/minute, targeting EtCO2 35-45 mmHg; avoid hyperventilation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Do not hyperventilate. Maintain a ventilation rate of 8-10 breaths per minute, targeting an EtCO2 of 35-45 mmHg
expectedActions.rationale: Hyperventilation reduces cerebral perfusion and can worsen post-arrest neurologic injury.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

expectedActions.shortAction: Monitor closely for recurrence of cardiac arrest using cardiac and EtCO2 monitoring and signs of perfusion
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Monitor closely for recurrence of cardiac arrest using clinical and adjunctive criteria such as cardiac monitoring, EtCO2 monitoring, and physical signs of perfusion
expectedActions.rationale: Post-ROSC patients remain at high risk for re-arrest during transport.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

phases.name: Airway obstruction not cleared
phases.description: Crew attempts bag-valve-mask ventilation without first visualizing and clearing the obstructing food bolus. No chest rise is achieved despite repeated ventilation attempts, and the patient's rhythm deteriorates toward asystole as hypoxia persists.
phases.triggerCondition: Ventilation was attempted without addressing the visible airway obstruction; without clearing the food bolus, positive pressure ventilation cannot move air past the obstruction, and the arrest progresses despite ongoing compressions.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Still obstructed; food debris remains visible, no chest rise with BVM attempts
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No palpable pulse despite ongoing compressions
otherFindings: No chest rise despite multiple BVM attempts
Food debris still visible at the airway, not addressed
EtCO2 remains critically low, consistent with ineffective ventilation

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize failed ventilation (no chest rise); reassess airway, perform direct laryngoscopy and suction to clear obstruction
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Airway obstruction with foreign body or swelling (e.g., angioedema, posterior pharyngeal and laryngeal infections). Suction airway: for significantly contaminated airways, consider utilizing a suction assisted laryngeal airway decontamination (SALAD) technique
expectedActions.rationale: Absence of chest rise despite BVM attempts should immediately prompt reassessment for an unaddressed airway obstruction rather than continued futile ventilation.
